before: After JSON parsing, require an object before reading named fields. Arrays and null need explicit rejection for this record-shaped request contract.
This exercise is a small pure JavaScript model. Its inputs are supplied directly; it does not receive live HTTP requests, operate a database, or deploy a service.

typeof null is "object", so the first comparison matters. Array.isArray detects arrays. The ! operator reverses its answer. This model accepts ordinary values produced by JSON.parse, not arbitrary class instances.

Read the function call isRecord({"title":"Moon"}) from the inside out: the arguments supply the inputs, isRecord runs the body once, and return sends its result back to the caller. console.log displays that result; it does not change it.
Why is typeof value === "object" insufficient by itself? Null and arrays satisfy that typeof comparison. Named-field requirements come after this guard.
after: Before reading a request's named fields, check its outer shape. Here, a record means an object with named fields. An array and null do not count as records for this rule.
This check is for ordinary values produced by JSON.parse. It checks the outside shape only. It does not prove that a required field exists or that its contents are valid.
JavaScript reports typeof null as "object". That is why value !== null must be checked separately. typeof value === "object" alone is not enough.
Array.isArray(value) tells you whether the value is an array. ! reverses that answer. The && operators require all three checks to pass before isRecord returns true.
Complete isRecord(value). Accept parsed JSON objects. Reject null, arrays, numbers, text, and true-or-false values. Leave the supplied value unchanged.
